229 Ministry of Mines (MoM) Kabadiwala Connect – Bringing the Informal Collector into the Formal Recycling Chain
Problem Statement Details
Problem Statement ID
26229
Problem Statement Title
Kabadiwala Connect – Bringing the Informal Collector into the Formal Recycling Chain
Description
Background: The overwhelming majority of India’s end-of-life electronics is collected through informal scrap dealers, waste-pickers, and local aggregators due to their extensive last-mile reach and low collection costs. However, these informal collectors remain largely outside the formal recycling ecosystem. The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 established a formal Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) framework involving authorized recyclers, but there is currently limited access for informal collectors to participate in this formal recycling chain. As a result, material collected by informal aggregators may undergo unsafe backyard processing such as open-air cable burning, acid leaching of printed circuit boards, and manual desoldering without proper extraction facilities. While materials such as copper and small quantities of gold may be recovered, valuable materials including lithium, cobalt, neodymium, tantalum, gallium, and indium may be lost. These practices also expose workers to significant health and safety risks. The fundamental gap is not only technological but also informational and institutional. Informal collectors may not know the prevailing fair price of materials, which nearby recyclers are authorized, how to complete a compliant material handover, or how to obtain a documented record of the transaction. Consequently, there is limited incentive for collectors to prefer the formal recycling route Problem: Design and develop a vernacular, low-literacy, offline-tolerant mobile platform that enables informal scrap collectors to discover fair prices, connect directly with authorized recyclers, complete a documented and traceable handover of collected materials, and receive payment. The platform should make the formal recycling channel an economically attractive and convenient option for informal collectors rather than creating an additional compliance burden The platform should: • Allow collectors to photograph, categorize, and create digital lots of collected materials such as CRTs, LCD panels, PCBs, cables, batteries, motors and magnet-bearing assemblies, and mixed plastics, enter approximate weight, and receive an instant value estimate. • Provide a price discovery and historical price dataset containing material category, sub-category,location, date, prevailing buying price, unit of measurement, approximate market range, and recycler/aggregator offered price. The system should use this dataset to provide transparent and current price information to collectors and identify basic price trends. • Maintain a material and transaction dataset containing lot/reference ID, material category, material description, photograph/image reference, approximate weight, estimated value, quoted price, final sale value, date and time of collection, collection location, recycler details, and transaction status. This dataset should enable traceability of material from collection to authorized recycling. • Maintain an authorized recycler/aggregator dataset containing recycler/aggregator name, facility location, materials accepted, authorization/registration details, authorization status, contact details, offered rates, pickup availability, and service area. The platform should use this information to identify and rank suitable authorized recyclers for a collector's lot. • Use the collected material image, category, weight, location, historical price, and transaction data to support AI/ML-based features such as material classification, approximate valuation, recycler matching, and identification of abnormal or inconsistent transaction values, wherever sufficient training data is available. • Provide current buying rates for different material categories and locations through a simple price board, including spoken price information and basic price trends. • Match collected lots with nearby authorized recyclers or aggregators based on location, material category, offered rate, pickup availability, and authorization status. • Generate a digital and verifiable handover/transfer record containing photographs, weight, timestamp, GPS/location details, and a unique reference that can be confirmed by the recycler. • Maintain an easy-to-understand earnings ledger showing transactions, payments, and pending dues, thereby building a usable financial and transaction history for collectors. • Provide pictorial and/or audio-based safety guidance on hazardous practices, including improper burning or opening of materials and safe handling of batteries and CRTs. • Support Marathi and Hindi at a minimum and provide a genuinely usable interface for users with limited literacy. • Operate in low-connectivity environments through an offline-first architecture, allowing core activities to be completed offline and synchronized when connectivity becomes available. • Support entry-level Android devices with a small application size and low memory requirements. Allow cash-based transactions while keeping digital payment optional and not making it a prerequisite for using the platform. Dataset Requirements: The solution should be designed to create and utilize structured datasets generated through field operations and platform transactions. The minimum dataset should cover the following: • Material Dataset: Material category, sub-category, material description, image, approximate weight, condition, source type, and estimated value. • Price Dataset: Material category, location, date/time, buying price, selling/quoted price, unit, recycler/aggregator, and historical price information. • Recycler Dataset: Recycler/facility name, location, materials accepted, authorization status/details,contact information, offered rate, pickup availability, and service area. • Transaction Dataset: Unique lot ID, collector ID, material category, quantity/weight, quoted price, final price, recycler ID, collection location, handover location, date/time, payment status, and transaction status. • Traceability Dataset: Lot ID, photographs, weight, timestamp, GPS/location, handover reference number, recycler confirmation, and subsequent transaction status. • Collector Dataset: A minimal profile containing collector ID, preferred language, general operating location, transaction history, and earnings history. The system should avoid collecting unnecessary personal information. • AI/ML Training Dataset: Where AI/ML functionality is proposed, teams should develop or use appropriately sourced datasets containing material images, material categories, weights, prices, locations, and transaction records for model training and validation. Teams should clearly identify the source, quality, size, and limitations of such datasets. • The dataset should support data cleaning, validation, anonymization where required, historical analysis, price prediction, material classification, recycler recommendation, and transaction-level traceability. • Teams should demonstrate how the dataset is generated, stored, validated, updated, and used by the application rather than treating the dataset as a static database. Expected Outcome: The proposed solution should create a simple digital bridge between informal collectors and the formal recycling ecosystem, improving price transparency, enabling traceable material handovers, connecting collectors with authorized recyclers, promoting safer handling practices, and encouraging greater participation in the formal recycling chain. The solution should include a working mobile application, recycler-side interface, structured datasets for materials, prices, recyclers and transactions, field research involving at least two working scrap collectors or aggregators, and a live usability demonstration. Teams should also provide a short unit-economics assessment comparing the collector's existing earnings with the potential earnings through the proposed platform and explaining how the platform can sustain its operations.

Background:

Food waste refers to the loss or disposal of edible food during production, processing, storage, distribution, retailing, and consumption stages. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), nearly one-third of the food produced globally for human consumption is wasted every year, resulting in significant financial losses, resource inefficiencies, and environmental degradation.

Description:

The economic repercussions of food waste on a global scale are substantial. The resources invested in producing, transporting, and processing wasted food contribute to increased production costs. Moreover, the disposal of food waste generates environmental and social costs. These include the emission of greenhouse gases during decomposition and the inefficient use of water, land, and energy resources (Alexander et al., 2017).

The economic impact of food waste in India extends beyond direct financial losses. The social costs are evident in the persistence of hunger and malnutrition, especially among vulnerable populations. Additionally, the environmental costs include the squandering of natural resources, such as water and arable land, contributing to ecological imbalances.

Food waste poses a significant challenge to the global and Indian economies, leading to economic losses, resource inefficiencies, and environmental degradation. Addressing this issue requires a multifaceted approach, including policy interventions and technological advancements.

There is a strong need for an intelligent, integrated, and real-time technological ecosystem that can predict food demand, identify surplus generation, optimise food redistribution, monitor food quality, reduce operational inefficiencies, and support sustainable food management practices across institutional food systems and food processing industries.

Develop an AI-powered Smart Food Waste Management and Redistribution Platform that integrates artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, IoT sensors, computer vision, and smart logistics systems to minimize food waste and optimize food resource utilization across institutional kitchens and food processing units.

The proposed system should be capable of:

  • Predicting food demand and surplus generation in real time using AI and historical consumption patterns.
  • Identifying food items nearing expiry or quality deterioration using smart sensors and image-based quality assessment.
  • Connecting surplus food with nearby NGOs, food banks, shelters, community kitchens, and secondary buyers through an automated redistribution network.
  • Optimizing transportation and delivery routes using AI-based logistics planning.
  • Monitoring processing efficiency, storage conditions, and operational performance in food processing units.
  • Detecting inefficiencies such as overproduction, raw material losses, machine downtime, and excessive energy usage.
  • Generating sustainability analytics including carbon footprint reduction, waste prevention metrics, resource efficiency indicators, and ESG compliance reports.
  • Supporting smart and data-driven production planning for institutional kitchens and food processing businesses.

The proposed AI-driven smart food management system has the potential to transform institutional food operations by creating a more efficient, sustainable, and socially responsible food ecosystem.

Through accurate demand forecasting and intelligent surplus management, the platform can substantially reduce food waste generated by institutional kitchens, cafeterias, catering services, and food businesses. By streamlining inventory planning, redistribution networks, and supply chain coordination, the system will improve overall food supply chain efficiency and minimise unnecessary resource consumption.

The platform will also assist organisations in achieving sustainability and ESG compliance by generating real-time analytics on waste reduction, carbon footprint savings, and responsible resource utilisation.

In addition, the solution will help improve food accessibility for economically vulnerable populations by enabling timely redistribution of surplus food to NGOs, shelters, and community organisations.

Institutions can further benefit from reduced operational costs, lower inventory losses, and optimised procurement decisions. Using AI-powered predictive insights, the platform will support smarter, data-driven food production planning, helping organisations move towards a circular, technology-enabled, and sustainable food management ecosystem.

237 Ministry of Defence Cryptographic Attribution and Immutable Decryption Provenance for Multi-Recipient Encrypted Document Distribution
Problem Statement Details
Problem Statement ID
26237
Problem Statement Title
Cryptographic Attribution and Immutable Decryption Provenance for Multi-Recipient Encrypted Document Distribution
Description

Description

Sensitive documents are often distributed under a broadcast-encrypt, individually-decrypt model, where a sender encrypts a file once and each recipient decrypts it independently using their own credentials.

When such a file is shared with a single recipient, a leak is trivially attributable. However, when the same file is distributed to a group of recipients, every recipient who was capable of decrypting it becomes an equally plausible suspect if the file leaks, since the decrypted content is identical for all of them and carries no trace of which specific decryption produced the leaked copy.

Existing safeguards such as server-side access logs and static watermarks applied before distribution do not solve this. Access logs can be altered by a privileged administrator, and a watermark that is identical across all recipients reproduces the same attribution problem it is meant to solve.

Expected Outcome

Teams are expected to build a system that generates a unique, invisible forensic watermark at the moment of decryption, specific to each recipient's session, so that every decrypted copy is visually identical but forensically distinct.

Each decryption event must be cryptographically bound to the recipient's identity using a digital signature generated with the recipient's own private key, so that the recipient cannot later deny having decrypted the file.

This signed decryption record must be committed to an immutable, tamper-evident ledger, so that no single administrator or compromised account can retroactively alter or erase the record of who decrypted what and when.

Given a leaked copy of a distributed document, the solution should be able to extract the embedded watermark, look it up against the ledger, and return a cryptographically verifiable record identifying the exact recipient responsible.

Key Requirements

  • Generate a unique, invisible forensic watermark at the moment of decryption.
  • Make the watermark specific to each recipient and decryption session.
  • Ensure every decrypted copy is visually identical while remaining forensically distinct.
  • Cryptographically bind each decryption event to the recipient's identity.
  • Use the recipient's own private key to generate a digital signature for the decryption record.
  • Use NIST-standardized post-quantum cryptographic algorithms instead of classical cryptographic algorithms for Key Exchange and Digital Signatures.
  • Implement the immutable audit layer using blockchain or Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT).
  • Ensure that no single administrator or compromised account can retroactively modify or delete audit records.
  • Extract the forensic watermark from a leaked document.
  • Look up the extracted watermark against the immutable ledger.
  • Return a cryptographically verifiable record identifying the recipient associated with the decryption event.
  • Support complete operation within an offline and air-gapped environment.
  • Have no dependency on external cloud KMS services.
  • Have no dependency on public blockchain networks.

End-to-End Workflow

  1. The sender encrypts the document and distributes it to authorized recipients.
  2. An authorized recipient decrypts the document using their credentials.
  3. The system generates a unique invisible forensic watermark tied to the recipient's decryption session.
  4. The recipient signs the decryption record using their post-quantum private signing key.
  5. The signed decryption record is committed to an offline, tamper-evident blockchain/DLT ledger.
  6. The recipient receives a visually identical but uniquely fingerprinted decrypted document.
  7. If the document is leaked, the forensic watermark is extracted from the leaked copy.
  8. The extracted watermark is matched against the immutable ledger.
  9. The associated post-quantum digital signature and ledger evidence are cryptographically verified.
  10. The system produces a verifiable record identifying the recipient and corresponding decryption event.

Deployment Constraint

The complete system must run fully within an offline and air-gapped environment. All cryptographic operations, identity management, watermark generation, ledger operations, and forensic verification must function without external cloud services, cloud KMS infrastructure, or public blockchain networks.

I. Description

A. Background

MoTA administers five scholarship schemes for Scheduled Tribe (ST) students, Pre-Matric, Post-Matric, Top Class, National Fellowship (NFST), and National Overseas Scholarship (NOS), spread across three disconnected systems: the National Scholarship Portal (NSP), the Scholarship Fellowship Management Portal / SFMP (Canara Bank), and the standalone NOS Portal. A student availing any scheme, or a family with children across schemes, must track applications, verification stages and disbursements separately, with no single view of scholarship status or funds received. Further, under the existing system, a student can avail only one scholarship/fellowship scheme at a time, making it important to have a unified view of the student’s existing scholarship status and eligibility before applying for another scheme.

The existing processes also involve multiple manual verification steps for identity, ST/PVTG status, income, academic records, institution details and other scheme-specific documents. The reform assessment identifies opportunities to digitally verify these details through existing government and institutional data sources such as DigiLocker, AISHE, UDISE+, APAAR, UIDAI, State e-District systems and UGC-NTA, thereby reducing repetitive documentation and processing delays.

B. Detailed Description

The problem statement envisages the development of a single, mobile-first Scholarship Module that enables ST students to access and track scholarship services across all five schemes through a common interface. The application should provide a consolidated view of scholarship applications, verification status, pending actions, sanctions and fund disbursements, while simplifying access to documents and providing timely notifications and assistance through the JAGO chatbot.

The solution should also enable API-based integration with existing scholarship and government data systems to support automated or semi-automated verification of applicant information. This may include verification of identity and ST/PVTG certificates, academic records and institution details, NET/JRF qualification, disability certificates, income and domicile certificates, and other documents applicable across the five schemes. The proposed architecture should enable the appropriate source system to be accessed through a common verification layer, with exceptions or mismatches routed for manual review rather than blocking the application.

The system should further support identification of ST students who are enrolled but not yet availing scholarship benefits, by enabling appropriate matching of scholarship registration data with UDISE+, APAAR and OTR information. This can help the Ministry identify gaps in scholarship coverage and enable targeted outreach to unreached beneficiaries.

The key challenge is therefore to create a unified student-facing experience across multiple existing scholarship systems while establishing a secure digital verification and information layer that reduces repetitive data submission, improves transparency and enables more timely processing.

C. Expected Solution

A unified mobile application for MoTA scholarship and fellowship schemes should be developed to provide students with a single platform for accessing and managing their scholarship-related services. The solution should:

  1. Scholarship Module: The proposed Scholarship Module should provide a unified dashboard covering all five scholarship schemes, enabling students to track applications from submission and verification through sanction and disbursement. It should include a digital document wallet with DigiLocker integration, allow reuse of previously submitted information and documents, and provide a consolidated view of payments, DBT status, pending actions and deficiencies.
  2. JAGO Chatbot: The solution should integrate scholarship services with the JAGO chatbot to provide information on eligibility, application status, required documents, deficiencies and disbursement. The chatbot should provide student-specific responses through integration with relevant scholarship systems, support multilingual interactions and send timely alerts on important application and payment milestones.
  3. Unified Verification & Integration Layer: The solution should integrate the existing scholarship systems and relevant government data sources to enable automated or semi-automated verification of applicant details and documents, with exceptions routed for manual review.

239 Ministry of Tribal Affairs AI-Enabled Scholarship and Fellowship Management System for Scheduled Tribes
Problem Statement Details
Problem Statement ID
26239
Problem Statement Title
AI-Enabled Scholarship and Fellowship Management System for Scheduled Tribes
Description

I. Description

A. Background

The Ministry of Tribal Affairs (MoTA) implements scholarship and fellowship schemes to provide financial assistance to Scheduled Tribe (ST) students pursuing higher education in India and abroad. These include schemes such as the National Fellowship for Scheduled Tribe (NFST) for eligible research programmes in India and the National Overseas Scholarship (NOS) for eligible Master's and Ph.D. programmes abroad.

The implementation of these schemes involves multiple stages, including applicant registration, online application, document submission, eligibility verification, scrutiny, screening, selection, communication, and post-selection/fellowship management. At present, several stages involve manual scrutiny, repeated correspondence and multiple levels of verification, resulting in processing delays, repetitive administrative effort, limited real-time visibility and scope for errors in verification and workflow management.

There is therefore a need for a common, secure, transparent and intelligent digital platform that can streamline the end-to-end administration of MoTA scholarship and fellowship schemes while allowing the scheme-specific eligibility, selection and documentation requirements to be configured within a common system.

B. Description

The problem statement envisages development of a single digital platform for end-to-end management of scholarship and fellowship schemes implemented by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs for Scheduled Tribe students.

It should bring the complete process, i.e., from application submission and eligibility verification to document scrutiny, selection, communication and post-selection management, onto one integrated system. It should be capable of handling the different eligibility criteria, documents and selection processes applicable to individual schemes through a configurable system.

Further, the platform should use automation and AI-based tools, wherever appropriate, to reduce manual verification, identify incomplete or deficient applications, support faster processing and improve the accuracy and transparency of the selection process.

Finally, the system should provide separate interfaces for applicants and administrators, enabling applicants to track their applications and respond to deficiencies, while enabling Ministry officials to monitor applications, verification, selection and scheme performance through dashboards and reports.

C. Expected Solution

An AI-enabled Scholarship and Fellowship Management System should be developed to provide an integrated digital workflow for managing scholarship and fellowship schemes implemented by MoTA for Scheduled Tribe students. The solution should:

  • Enable end-to-end digital application management, covering application submission, document upload, eligibility verification, scrutiny, selection and communication.
  • Automate and support eligibility and document verification using configurable scheme-specific rules and AI-based tools such as OCR/document intelligence, wherever appropriate.
  • Support transparent screening and selection by applying approved scheme criteria to identify eligible applicants and assist in merit-based selection, while retaining appropriate human oversight.
  • Provide application tracking and workflow management for applicants and administrators, including deficiency identification, communication, resubmission and status tracking.
  • Provide dashboards and analytics to enable MoTA to monitor applications, verification, selection and scheme performance across relevant parameters.

The overarching goal is to improve the overall efficiency, transparency and accountability of MoTA's scholarship and fellowship administration by reducing manual effort, accelerating processing, improving verification accuracy and providing a seamless digital experience for applicants and administrators.

240 Ministry of Tribal Affairs AI-Based Spring Revival and Recharge Planning for Tribal Areas
Problem Statement Details
Problem Statement ID
26240
Problem Statement Title
AI-Based Spring Revival and Recharge Planning for Tribal Areas
Description

I. Description

A. Background

Springs are an important source of water for communities in hilly and tribal regions. The availability and sustainability of spring water depends on the recharge of the underlying aquifer. However, the recharge zone from which rainfall contributes to a particular spring is often difficult to identify through surface observations alone.

Groundwater movement is influenced by terrain, geological structures, slope, drainage patterns, rainfall and land-use characteristics. Identification of the recharge zone and selection of suitable locations for recharge interventions therefore requires integration of multiple spatial and hydrogeological parameters along with field-based assessment.

At present, identification of recharge zones and suitable locations for recharge interventions often requires site-specific field surveys and specialised hydrogeological expertise. This can be time-consuming and difficult to scale across remote and geographically challenging tribal areas. There is a need for a technology-enabled decision-support mechanism that can help field agencies identify and prioritise potential recharge areas and intervention sites using available data.

B. Description

The above problem statement envisages development of an AI/ML-enabled geospatial decision-support system to assist in delineating the probable recharge zone of a spring and prioritising suitable locations for spring-revival interventions.

The system should be capable of integrating spatial, geological, hydrogeological, climatic and field datasets, including:

  • Geological structures such as strike, dip, fractures, faults and joints
  • Spring characteristics such as location, elevation, discharge and seasonal behaviour
  • Terrain parameters derived from Digital Elevation Models (DEM), slope, aspect, elevation and drainage
  • Geological formations, rock types and geological contacts
  • Rainfall, runoff and spring-discharge trends
  • Land-use/land-cover information
  • Existing water conservation and recharge structures
  • Field observations and community-generated information, wherever available

The system should analyse these datasets to identify spatial patterns associated with potential recharge areas and generate probability-based estimates of recharge suitability. It should be capable of working with varying levels of data availability and quality, while indicating the level of confidence associated with its outputs.

The system should also support field verification of identified recharge areas and proposed intervention sites, allowing field observations and subsequent spring-discharge information to be incorporated for assessment and improvement of the model.

C. Expected Solution

An AI-powered Spring Recharge Zone Identification and Decision Support System should be developed to support evidence-based planning and prioritisation of spring-revival interventions in tribal and hilly areas. The solution should:

  • Identify probable recharge zones/springsheds using available spatial, geological, hydrogeological, climatic and field datasets, with appropriate indication of confidence or uncertainty.
  • Generate recharge suitability and priority maps to identify and rank areas with higher potential for groundwater recharge and spring revival interventions.
  • Identify suitable intervention locations and provide indicative recommendations for appropriate recharge measures based on relevant site characteristics.
  • Flag potentially unsuitable or high-risk locations, including areas where interventions may have limited effectiveness or potential geological/landslide risks.
  • Provide an interactive GIS-based interface and field-validation mechanism to enable field agencies to visualise outputs, validate identified locations and incorporate subsequent observations and spring-discharge data.

The overarching goal is to improve the efficiency, scalability and evidence base of spring-revival planning by enabling government agencies to identify probable recharge zones and prioritise technically suitable groundwater recharge interventions, particularly in remote and tribal areas.

-# SIH26073-Weather
-AI/ML-based intelligent anomaly detection for Automatic Weather Stations (SIH26073). Detects sensor faults (drift, flatline, spike, dropout) vs real weather events using per-station anomaly scoring + cross-station correlation. Live dashboard with station health map, alerts & charts. Built for SIH 2026, Ministry of Earth Sciences.
+# SIH26073 — Anomaly Detection for Automatic Weather Stations
+
+Built for Smart India Hackathon 2026 (Ministry of Earth Sciences, problem statement SIH26073). A two-stage pipeline that tells the difference between a broken sensor and a real weather event — something IMD's current rule-based checks can't reliably do.
+
+## Problem
+
+Automatic Weather Stations fail in specific, well-known ways: sensor drift, flatlining, spikes, and dropouts. A naive threshold check flags all of these as "anomalies" but can't tell a faulty station from a genuine, spatially-spreading weather event (e.g. a real storm front pushing wind speed up across several stations at once). Treating both the same way means either drowning operators in false alerts or missing real events buried in sensor noise.
+
+## Architecture
+
+```
+Sensor reading (per station, per timestep)
+    → AnomalyDetector: rolling per-station z-score scoring
+        - spike check      (|z| ≥ threshold)
+        - flatline check   (last 7 readings identical)
+        - drift check      (short-window mean vs long-window baseline)
+    → is_anomaly? → FaultClassifier: cross-station spatial correlation
+        - find neighbouring stations within 50km (haversine distance)
+        - check if neighbours show a correlated anomaly on the same parameter
+        - isolated anomaly  → SENSOR_FAULT
+        - correlated anomaly → REAL_EVENT
+    → verdict + confidence + human-readable reason
+```
+
+The classifier's core idea is the actual differentiator: a lone station spiking on wind speed with quiet neighbours is almost certainly a faulty anemometer. The same spike showing up on three neighbouring stations at once is a storm front.
+
+## Detection Method
+
+Per-station, per-parameter rolling z-score (window size 50, minimum 10 readings before trusting the stats — avoids false alarms while a station is still "warming up"). Chosen deliberately over a black-box model for this stage: no training data required beyond a short normal-baseline window per station, and it's fully explainable — every flag traces back to a specific mean/std deviation, which matters when the output has to be defensible to hackathon judges and, eventually, real meteorologists. An `IsolationForest`-based drop-in variant exists in the same file as a stretch path if per-station data volume grows enough to justify it.
+
+## Classification Method
+
+For each flagged anomaly, the classifier looks up neighbouring stations by great-circle distance and checks whether they were also recently anomalous on the same parameter. If ≥40% of checked neighbours agree, it's called a real event; otherwise, a sensor fault. Confidence scales continuously with how far the agreement ratio sits from that threshold in either direction, rather than being a flat number — a 0-of-4-neighbours-agreeing isolated spike reads with much higher confidence than a 1-of-4 borderline case.
+
+## Validated Against Ground Truth
+
+Ran the full pipeline against a synthetic multi-station dataset with known-planted faults. All 8 planted scenarios were caught correctly:
+
+- Isolated wind-speed **spike** at a single station (correctly classified as sensor fault)
+- Slow **pressure drift** over a 15-timestep window (correctly flagged and classified)
+- **Flatline** on temperature (correctly distinguished from a genuine steady reading)
+- Station **dropout** (missing rows for a 5-timestep window) — verified no crash and no false alert generated during the gap
+- A genuine 3-station **correlated wind event** — all three stations independently flagged and correctly classified as `real_event` with matching confidence, rather than three separate false sensor-fault alerts
+
+Full run across the test dataset: 47 total alerts generated, breaking down to 28 sensor faults, 18 real events, 1 uncertain (a station with no neighbours in range to cross-check against — correctly reported as low-confidence rather than guessing).
+
+## Tech Stack
+
+`Python` `NumPy-free rolling statistics` (dependency-light by design for the detector stage) `scikit-learn` (optional IsolationForest path) `pytest`
+
+## Status
+
+Detector and classifier are both implemented, unit-tested (`tests/test_classifier_edges.py`, `tests/test_fault_types.py`), and validated end-to-end against a planted-fault synthetic dataset via `run_on_dataset.py`. Live dashboard (station health map, alerts, charts) is scoped for the SIH pitch but sits outside this backend repo's current contents.
+
+---
+
+*Detection and classification logic, spatial correlation approach, and the ground-truth validation harness are original work for the SIH26073 submission.*"}]}

+# SkyGuard AI — Project Status & Progress Report
+
+**Status date:** 2026-09-29 · **Branch:** `feat/skyguard-sih-prototype` · **Latest commit:** `8ad71df` · **Working tree:** clean (not pushed)
+
+**Overall status: production-oriented SIH prototype — VERIFIED** (Docker: environment-unverified · ESP32: hardware-unverified)
+
+SkyGuard AI is a real-time, explainable anomaly-detection layer for Automatic Weather Station **temperature, pressure and
+relative humidity**, built for remote Indian stations. It checks each observation, gives each alert a calibrated probability,
+a fault pattern, a severity and a plain-language explanation, and keeps a sensor-health score. It tells regional weather
+apart from single-station sensor faults, suggests corrected values without ever overwriting raw data, and works with stations
+that go offline and upload later. A live dashboard and a tiny C edge-check library for ESP32-class loggers are included.
+
+All figures below come from files in `artifacts/`. The detailed reports are in `docs/reports/`.
+

+## 3. Key results (v2 frozen final test — evaluated once)
+
+The test set has 94,367 hourly observations from 22 Indian stations, including 4 stations never seen in training (VOBG, VOTV,
+VIJP, VOPB). Seed and injection profile are unseen, and the SHA-256 was verified at evaluation.
+
+| Metric | SkyGuard Hybrid |
+|---|---:|
+| Precision | **0.820** |
+| Recall (row-level) | 0.457 |
+| F1 | 0.587 |
+| PR-AUC / ROC-AUC | **0.688 / 0.903** |
+| False alerts per station-day | **0.184** |
+| Event-level recall | **90.1%** |
+| Regional weather events wrongly alerted | **13.4%** |
+| Fault-pattern macro-F1 | 0.562 |
+| Calibration: Brier / ECE | 0.040 / 0.009 |
+| Held-out stations F1 (vs seen stations) | 0.577 (vs 0.589) |
+
+> Row-level recall counts individual anomalous observations that were flagged. Event-level recall counts whether an injected
+> event was detected at least once. That is why one is 0.46 and the other 90%.
+
+### Baseline comparison (same test data)
+
+| Approach | F1 | PR-AUC |
+|---|---:|---:|
+| Fixed thresholds | 0.205 | 0.173 |
+| Robust statistical (z-score) | 0.215 | 0.249 |
+| Isolation Forest | 0.280 | 0.393 |
+| Temporal autoencoder (MLP) | 0.242 | 0.273 |
+| **SkyGuard Hybrid** | **0.587** | **0.688** |
+
+### What the pass-2 decision rules changed (same model, same v2 data)
+
+| | Without the new rules | **With the new rules (deployed)** |
+|---|---:|---:|
+| Regional events wrongly alerted | 43.3% | **13.4%** |
+| False alerts per station-day | 0.464 | **0.184** |
+| Precision | 0.701 | **0.820** |
+| Event recall | 95.0% | 90.1% |
+| Row-level recall | 0.592 | 0.457 |
+
+Drift and step alerts now wait for sustained evidence. That costs some row-level recall and buys far fewer false alarms.
+
+### Other measurements
+
+- **Correction accuracy** (mean absolute error of the recommended value vs the true value): temperature 2.03 °C, pressure 1.43 hPa, humidity 8.25 %.
+- **Real-time latency** (full engine, one observation at a time, this PC): p50 340 ms, p95 538 ms, p99 632 ms; ~2.9 observations/s. Batched uploads are much faster per observation.
+- **Edge C library** (cross-compiled for the ESP32-C3 instruction set): 1,134 bytes flash, 28 B state per station, 96 B worst-case stack, ~250 ns per observation on the host PC (not on an ESP32).

+## 5. Known limitations (open items)
+
+1. **Docker not verified.** Docker isn't installed on this machine. Install Docker Desktop, then run `python scripts/verify_docker.py`.
+2. **No physical ESP32 test** and no energy or battery measurement. The edge library is validated by cross-compilation and host execution only.
+3. **Proxy data.** Observations are Indian aerodrome METAR reports from the Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive, **not** the IMD AWS network feed. Temperature resolution is 1 °C and pressure is QNH.
+4. **Regional false alerts.** 13.4% on the unseen test, above the 10% target that was met on validation.
+5. **Row-level recall is modest (0.457).** Drift and step alerts are deliberately delayed until confirmed.
+6. **Latency** is a few hundred ms per live observation (pandas-based). That's fine for hourly data but not optimised.
+7. **Prototype architecture.** SQLite in a single process; PostgreSQL and horizontal scaling are the documented next step.
+8. **Scenario G criterion changed** in pass 2, from comparing raw probabilities to checking the final decision. This is disclosed in the reports.

+# SkyGuard AI
+
+Real-time, explainable anomaly detection for **temperature, atmospheric pressure and relative humidity** from
+Automatic Weather Stations, designed for remote and data-sparse Indian deployments.
+
+It is a **production-oriented SIH prototype** (not production infrastructure) that takes AWS observations and turns them into verified alerts:
+
+* **Checks:** deterministic QC, then temporal, multivariate and spatial evidence, feeding a calibrated anomaly probability.
+* **Per alert:** an observable fault pattern, severity, explanation and sensor-health score.
+* **Correction:** an optional correction *recommendation*. The raw value is always preserved.
+* **Operations:** store-and-forward remote uplink, a live dashboard, and a tiny C edge-check library for ESP32-class loggers.
+
+Measured results are in [`docs/reports/`](docs/reports/), generated from `artifacts/` by `scripts/make_report.py`:
+
+* [Final SIH evaluation report](docs/reports/SkyGuard_AI_Final_SIH_Evaluation_Report.md)
+* [Weather-vs-sensor analysis](docs/reports/SkyGuard_AI_Weather_vs_Sensor_Analysis.md)
+* [Deployment verification](docs/reports/SkyGuard_AI_Final_Deployment_Verification.md)
+
+The README deliberately repeats no numbers.
+
+## Architecture
+
+```text
+AWS logger ─ edge C checks (edge/firmware) ─ StationClient store-and-forward buffer (edge/station_client.py)
+      │  HTTP(S), batched, idempotent
+      ▼
+FastAPI  backend/app.py ── typed Pydantic payloads, size/rate limits, CORS
+      ▼
+StreamEngine  ml/stream.py   (same code as batch evaluation → training/serving parity, tested)
+  deterministic QC (ml/qc.py, config/skyguard.toml)
+  → temporal features (past-only, station time-of-day baseline)     ml/features.py
+  → multivariate T/P/RH consistency (dew-point physics)
+  → spatial features from configurable neighbours (optional)
+  → MLP temporal autoencoder → gradient-boosted detector → isotonic calibration   ml/models.py
+  → fault-pattern + parameter classifiers
+  → weather-vs-sensor decision layer (ml/decision.py): regional evidence score, station exceptions,
+    persistence-confirmed DRIFT/STEP — parameters selected on validation
+  → severity · explanation · sensor health · correction · maintenance risk        ml/postprocess.py
+      ▼
+SQLite (raw values immutable via trigger)  ──  SSE /api/v1/stream  ──  React dashboard (dashboard/)
+```
+
+The model inputs are T, P and RH only. Latitude and longitude are used solely to choose neighbours. Nothing names a station
+in the code; stations, neighbours (radius and cap), thresholds and windows all come from `config/skyguard.toml`.
+
+## Repository layout
+
+| Path | Contents |
+|---|---|
+| `config/skyguard.toml` | versioned configuration (QC rules, windows, split, seeds, severity, health) |
+| `data/raw/iem_metar/` | raw observations exactly as downloaded (gzip) + `PROVENANCE.json` |
+| `data/processed/` | canonical dataset + station registry (generated) |
+| `data/benchmark/` | train / val / **frozen** `final_eval` benchmarks + manifests |
+| `data/demo/` | deterministic SIH demo replay + its ground truth |
+| `injection/` | reproducible anomaly injector |
+| `ml/` | QC, features, models, stream engine, post-processing, evaluation |
+| `backend/` | FastAPI app, SQLite store, replay runner |
+| `dashboard/` | React + Vite dashboard |
+| `edge/` | C99 edge checks, ESP32 sketch, host harness, station uplink simulator |
+| `scripts/` | data, benchmark, training, evaluation, replay, scenarios, report |
+| `tests/` | unit / integration / ml / e2e |
+| `artifacts/` | final model, validation selection, final evaluation, scenarios, edge metrics |
+
+## Data provenance
+
+The real Indian observations are **IMD aerodrome METAR reports**, retrieved from the Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive
+(network `IN__ASOS`). `scripts/fetch_raw_data.py` records the URL, retrieval time and SHA-256 of every file, and raw files are never modified. Some limits of this source:
+
+* It is an AWS-like surface observation stream, **not** the IMD AWS network feed.
+* Temperature resolution is 1 °C.
+* Pressure is the QNH altimeter setting.
+* ESSDP/INCOIS, NCAOR, Meghalaya and IMD DSP were evaluated but are not openly bulk-downloadable from this environment; the report gives the reasons.
+
+The core demo needs no internet access: raw data, the demo stream and the trained model are all local.
+

+

+python -m venv .venv

+## Reproduce everything (exact commands)
+
+```bash
+python scripts/fetch_raw_data.py          # only step needing internet; skipped files already in data/raw
+python scripts/build_dataset.py           # raw -> data/processed/clean.csv + stations.json
+python scripts/inject_anomalies.py --input data/processed/clean.csv --output data/benchmark.csv --seed 42   # stand-alone injector
+python scripts/build_benchmark.py         # leakage-safe splits; FREEZES final_eval (v1) and final_eval_v2 (re-run = integrity check)
+python scripts/train.py                   # trains baselines + ablation variants on TRAIN, selects on VALIDATION
+python scripts/evaluate.py                # validation report -> artifacts/validation/
+python scripts/diagnose_validation.py     # weather-vs-sensor / drift diagnostics on validation -> artifacts/regression/
+python scripts/evaluate_final.py --dataset data/benchmark/final_eval_v2 --model artifacts/final_model
+python edge/build_edge.py                 # C edge library + RV32 size/stack + host timing -> artifacts/edge/
+python scripts/build_demo.py              # deterministic SIH demo replay -> data/demo/
+python scripts/verify_docker.py           # Docker build/run/health/smoke, or ENVIRONMENT-UNVERIFIED if no engine
+python -m pytest tests -q --junitxml artifacts/regression/pytest_junit.xml
+python scripts/make_report.py             # docs/reports/*.md from artifacts
+```
+
+Order matters: the final benchmark is frozen **before** training (v2 was frozen before the hardening pass; v1 is kept, historical). `train.py` refuses to run otherwise, and it records the
+benchmark hash and freeze time in the model metadata. `evaluate_final.py` verifies both before evaluating.

+## Replay and scenarios
+
+* **Dashboard:** choose `sih_demo`, then *Start replay*. There's an 8-day warm-up, then 72 live hours.
+* **CLI replay over HTTP:** `python scripts/replay.py --input data/demo/sih_demo.csv --speed 3600`
+* **SIH scenarios A–J against a running API:** `python scripts/run_scenarios.py --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000`. Evidence is written to `artifacts/scenarios/scenario_results.json`.

+## API (all payloads typed; see http://localhost:8000/docs)
+
+| Method | Path | Purpose |
+|---|---|---|
+| GET | `/api/v1/health` | service, model and DB state, detector mode |
+| GET | `/api/v1/stations`, `/api/v1/stations/{id}` | status, health, maintenance, neighbours |
+| GET | `/api/v1/health/stations` | sensor-health summary |
+| POST | `/api/v1/observations` | one observation or `{"observations": [...]}` batch (≤ 5000) |
+| GET | `/api/v1/observations/latest`, `/api/v1/observations/history` | stored raw + results |
+| GET/PATCH | `/api/v1/anomalies`, `/api/v1/anomalies/{id}` | alerts; operator review state |
+| GET | `/api/v1/metrics` | latency p50/p95/p99, throughput, CPU/RAM, distributions |
+| POST | `/api/v1/replay/start`, `/api/v1/replay/stop`; GET `/api/v1/replay/status`, `/api/v1/replay/scenarios` | demo replay |
+| POST | `/api/v1/admin/reset` | clear processed state for a reproducible demo |
+| GET | `/api/v1/stream` | Server-Sent Events: live updates without page refresh |
+
+### Semantics
+
+* **`anomaly_probability`**: isotonic-calibrated on validation data (Brier score and reliability curve are reported).
+* **`anomaly_score`**: the uncalibrated detector output. It is not a probability.
+* **Deterministic QC hits** (missing, sentinel, impossible range) are reported as probability 1.0 with detector `deterministic_qc`.
+* **No model available:** the API runs an explicit `qc_only_fallback` mode. It reports no probability, and the dashboard shows a red banner.
+* **Delayed or out-of-order records** are accepted and scored on the history that precedes their *observation* time. Duplicates are idempotent.
+* **Severity** is `score = 40·p + 20·min(|z|/10,1) + 15·min(persistence/6,1) + 10·(n_vars−1)/2 + 10·spatial_isolation + 5·qc_hard`, with levels MEDIUM ≥ 45, HIGH ≥ 65 and CRITICAL ≥ 82 (`config/skyguard.toml [severity]`).
+* **Sensor health** is 100 minus weighted 24-hour rates of anomalies, missing data, flatline, drift/offset and communication gaps. It is a data-quality score, not a hardware diagnosis. Statuses: NORMAL ≥ 85, WATCH ≥ 70, DEGRADED ≥ 50, then CRITICAL.
+* **Maintenance risk** is LOW, MEDIUM or HIGH with a reason, or "Insufficient history". It never predicts a time to failure.
+
+## Security
+
+* **Demo authentication:** disabled for the temporary SIH evaluation deployment.
+* **Secrets:** none are committed.
+* **Input limits:** strict Pydantic validation, a 2 MB body limit, a 5000-record batch limit, and a per-client write rate limit.
+* **Other controls:** configured CORS and safe logging.
+* **Public deployment:** HTTPS should be used for any deployment exposed beyond the temporary demo.
+
+## Docker
+
+```bash
+cp .env.example .env
+```
+```bash
+docker compose up --build
+```
+
+This is a single container (dashboard, API and edge library) with a named volume for the database and a health check. `python scripts/verify_docker.py` performs and records the verification; on the build machine no Docker engine was installed, so the container is **environment-unverified** (see the deployment verification report).
+
+## Tests
+
+```bash
+python -m pytest tests -q
+```
+
+The unit, integration, ml and e2e suites are all included. The e2e tests start a real uvicorn server and run the SIH scenarios over HTTP.
+
+## Known limitations
+
+See section 13 of the evaluation report. In brief:
+
+* **Data:** METAR resolution and pressure type, and injected rather than real labelled faults.
+* **Spatial coverage:** evidence exists only where neighbours are within the configured radius.
+* **Weather vs sensor:** some regional weather events still raise an alert; the decision layer trades some row-level recall for far fewer false alerts (quantified in the reports).
+* **Edge:** ESP32-compatible C edge library validated by cross-compilation and host execution; no physical ESP32 hardware validation or energy measurement.
+* **Docker:** not verified on the build machine (no engine installed).

+"""SkyGuard AI API.  uvicorn backend.app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
+
+Environment (see .env.example): SKYGUARD_CORS_ORIGINS, SKYGUARD_DB,
+SKYGUARD_MODEL_DIR, SKYGUARD_STATIONS, SKYGUARD_DEMO_DIR, SKYGUARD_WRITE_RATE_PER_MIN.
+"""
+import os
+
+# single-row inference: avoid OpenMP thread spin-up per call (set before sklearn loads)
+os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "1")
+
+import asyncio
+import json
+import logging
+import sqlite3
+import time
+from collections import deque
+from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
+from pathlib import Path
+
+import psutil
+from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Query, Request
+from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
+from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse, StreamingResponse
+from fastapi.staticfiles import StaticFiles
+
+from backend.db import DB
+from backend.replay import ReplayRunner
+from backend.schemas import (AnomalyOut, AnomalyUpdate, BatchIn, HealthOut, IngestResponse, ObservationIn,
+                             ObservationResult, ReplayStart, StationOut)
+from ml.config import ROOT, load_config
+from ml.evaluation import latency_stats
+from ml.pipeline import ModelBundle, load_stations
+from ml.stream import StreamEngine
+
+log = logging.getLogger("skyguard")
+logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s")
+CFG = load_config()
+
+
+def env(name: str, default: str) -> str:
+    return os.environ.get(name, default)
+
+
+class State:
+    def __init__(self):
+        self.db = DB(env("SKYGUARD_DB", str(ROOT / "data" / "skyguard.db")))
+        self.stations = load_stations(Path(env("SKYGUARD_STATIONS", str(ROOT / "data" / "processed" / "stations.json"))))
+        self.bundle, self.model_error = None, None
+        try:
+            self.bundle = ModelBundle.load(Path(env("SKYGUARD_MODEL_DIR", str(ROOT / "artifacts" / "final_model"))))
+        except Exception as e:  # explicit, labelled fallback - never a silent substitution
+            self.model_error = f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"
+            log.error("model unavailable, running qc_only_fallback: %s", self.model_error)
+        self.engine = StreamEngine(self.stations, self.bundle, CFG)
+        self.db.upsert_stations(self.stations)
+        self.latency = deque(maxlen=20000)       # engine processing latency (ms)
+        self.e2e = deque(maxlen=20000)           # request-side latency incl. DB + publish (ms)
+        self.done_at = deque(maxlen=100000)      # wall-clock completion times for throughput
+        self.subscribers: set[asyncio.Queue] = set()
+        self.loop: asyncio.AbstractEventLoop | None = None
+        self.started = time.time()
+        self.rate: dict[str, deque] = {}
+        self.replay = ReplayRunner(self)
+
+    def reset(self) -> None:
+        self.db.reset()
+        self.engine = StreamEngine(self.stations, self.bundle, CFG)
+        self.latency.clear(), self.e2e.clear(), self.done_at.clear()
+
+    def publish(self, event: str, data: dict) -> None:
+        if not self.loop:
+            return
+        msg = f"event: {event}\ndata: {json.dumps(data, default=str)}\n\n"
+        for q in list(self.subscribers):
+            self.loop.call_soon_threadsafe(_offer, q, msg)
+
+    def ingest(self, observations: list[dict], quiet: bool = False) -> list[dict]:
+        """Shared ingestion path for the API, the replay engine and the station simulator."""
+        t0 = time.perf_counter()
+        results = self.engine.process_many(observations)
+        src = {o["station_id"]: o.get("source") for o in observations}
+        for r in results:
+            if r["status"] != "accepted":
+                continue
+            try:
+                self.db.insert_result(r, src.get(r["station_id"]))
+            except sqlite3.Error as e:
+                for x in results:  # keep engine and DB consistent: nothing from this request counts as ingested
+                    if x["status"] == "accepted":
+                        self.engine.forget(x["station_id"], x["observation_time"])
+                log.error("database error on insert: %s", type(e).__name__)
+                raise HTTPException(503, "database unavailable; observations not stored, retry later") from e
+        for rv in self.engine.pop_revisions():
+            self.db.apply_revision(rv)
+            if not quiet:
+                self.publish("revision", {k: rv[k] for k in ("station_id", "observation_time", "was_anomaly", "is_anomaly", "fault_pattern")})
+        per = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000 / max(1, len(results))
+        now = time.time()
+        for r in results:
+            if r["status"] != "accepted":
+                continue
+            self.latency.append(r["processing_latency_ms"])
+            self.e2e.append(per)
+            self.done_at.append(now)
+            if not quiet:
+                self.publish("observation", _compact(r))
+                if r["is_anomaly"] or r.get("gap_event") or r.get("regional_suppressed"):
+                    self.publish("anomaly", {"station_id": r["station_id"], "observation_time": r["observation_time"],
+                                             "fault_pattern": r["fault_pattern"], "severity": r["severity"],
+                                             "regional_suppressed": r.get("regional_suppressed"), "gap": bool(r.get("gap_event"))})
+        return results
+
+
+def _offer(q: asyncio.Queue, msg: str) -> None:
+    if not q.full():
+        q.put_nowait(msg)
+
+
+def _compact(r: dict) -> dict:
+    keys = ["station_id", "observation_time", "ingestion_time", "temperature_c", "pressure_hpa", "relative_humidity_pct",
+            "is_anomaly", "anomaly_probability", "fault_pattern", "parameter", "severity", "health_score", "health_status",
+            "estimated_temperature_c", "estimated_pressure_hpa", "estimated_relative_humidity_pct", "regional_evidence",
+            "regional_suppressed", "weather_status", "delayed", "out_of_order", "processing_latency_ms", "edge_flags", "edge_health_score"]
+    return {k: r.get(k) for k in keys}
+
+
+S: State | None = None
+
+
+@asynccontextmanager
+async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
+    global S
+    S = State()
+    S.loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
+    log.info("SkyGuard API ready: %d stations, mode=%s", len(S.stations), S.engine.mode)
+    yield
+    S.replay.stop()
+
+
+app = FastAPI(title="SkyGuard AI", version="1.0.0", lifespan=lifespan,
+              description="Real-time anomaly detection for Automatic Weather Stations (T, P, RH).")
+app.add_middleware(CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=[o.strip() for o in env(
+    "SKYGUARD_CORS_ORIGINS", "http://localhost:5173,http://127.0.0.1:5173").split(",") if o.strip()],
+                   allow_methods=["GET", "POST", "PATCH"], allow_headers=["Authorization", "Content-Type"])
+
+
+@app.middleware("http")
+async def limits(request: Request, call_next):
+    """Upload size limit and per-client write rate limit (safe logging: no payloads, no tokens)."""
+    if request.method in ("POST", "PATCH"):
+        cl = request.headers.get("content-length")
+        if cl is None or not cl.isdigit():
+            if request.url.path.startswith("/api/v1/observations"):
+                return JSONResponse({"detail": "Content-Length required"}, status_code=411)
+        elif int(cl) > CFG["api"]["max_body_bytes"]:
+            return JSONResponse({"detail": f"payload exceeds {CFG['api']['max_body_bytes']} bytes"}, status_code=413)
+        limit = int(env("SKYGUARD_WRITE_RATE_PER_MIN", "600"))
+        key = request.client.host if request.client else "unknown"
+        q = S.rate.setdefault(key, deque())
+        now = time.time()
+        while q and now - q[0] > 60:
+            q.popleft()
+        if len(q) >= limit:
+            return JSONResponse({"detail": "rate limit exceeded"}, status_code=429)
+        q.append(now)
+    return await call_next(request)
+
+
+# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ health
+@app.get("/api/v1/health", response_model=HealthOut)
+def health():
+    try:
+        S.db.query("SELECT 1")
+        db_ok = True
+    except sqlite3.Error:
+        db_ok = False
+    md = S.bundle.metadata if S.bundle else {}
+    return HealthOut(status="ok" if db_ok else "degraded", model_loaded=S.bundle is not None, detector_mode=S.engine.mode,
+                     model_version=f"{md.get('feature_version')}/{md.get('selected_variant')}/{md.get('trained_at')}" if md else None,
+                     database_ok=db_ok, stations=len(S.stations), auth_required_for_writes=False)
+
+
+def _active_counts() -> dict:
+    rows = S.db.query("SELECT station_id, COUNT(*) n, SUM(severity='CRITICAL') c FROM anomalies a WHERE state IN ('OPEN','ACKNOWLEDGED') "
+                      "AND observation_time >= (SELECT datetime(MAX(o.observation_time), '-2 hours') FROM observations o WHERE o.station_id=a.station_id) "
+                      "GROUP BY station_id")
+    return {r["station_id"]: (r["n"], r["c"] or 0) for r in rows}
+
+
+def _station(sid: str, active: dict) -> StationOut:
+    return StationOut(**S.engine.station_summary(sid), active_anomalies=active.get(sid, (0, 0))[0],
+                      active_critical=active.get(sid, (0, 0))[1])
+
+
+@app.get("/api/v1/stations", response_model=list[StationOut])
+def stations():
+    active = _active_counts()
+    return [_station(s, active) for s in sorted(S.stations)]
+
+
+@app.get("/api/v1/stations/{station_id}", response_model=StationOut)
+def station(station_id: str):
+    if station_id not in S.stations:
+        raise HTTPException(404, "unknown station")
+    return _station(station_id, _active_counts())
+
+
+@app.get("/api/v1/health/stations")
+def station_health():
+    return [{k: v for k, v in S.engine.station_summary(s).items() if k in (
+        "station_id", "health_score", "health_status", "health_reasons", "maintenance", "status", "label")} for s in sorted(S.stations)]
+
+
+# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ observations
+@app.post("/api/v1/observations", response_model=IngestResponse)
+def post_observations(payload: BatchIn | ObservationIn):
+    obs = payload.observations if isinstance(payload, BatchIn) else [payload]
+    if len(obs) > CFG["api"]["max_batch"]:
+        raise HTTPException(413, "batch too large")
+    res = S.ingest([o.model_dump(mode="json") for o in obs])
+    return IngestResponse(accepted=sum(r["status"] == "accepted" for r in res),
+                          duplicates=sum(r["status"] == "duplicate" for r in res),
+                          rejected=sum(r["status"] == "rejected" for r in res),
+                          results=[ObservationResult(**r) for r in res])
+
+
+def _obs_row(r: dict) -> dict:
+    r = dict(r)
+    for k in ("delayed", "out_of_order", "is_anomaly", "regional_evidence", "regional_suppressed", "replacement_recommended"):
+        r[k] = bool(r[k]) if r.get(k) is not None else None

+    return r
+
+
+@app.get("/api/v1/observations/latest")
+def latest(station_id: str | None = None):
+    sql = ("SELECT o.* FROM observations o JOIN (SELECT station_id, MAX(observation_time) t FROM observations GROUP BY station_id) m "

+    rows = S.db.query(sql + (" WHERE o.station_id=?" if station_id else ""), (station_id,) if station_id else ())
+    return [_obs_row(r) for r in rows]
+
+
+@app.get("/api/v1/observations/history")
+def history(station_id: str, start: str | None = None, end: str | None = None, limit: int = Query(500, ge=1, le=5000)):
+    sql, args = "SELECT * FROM observations WHERE station_id=?", [station_id]
+    if start:
+        sql, args = sql + " AND observation_time>=?", args + [start]
+    if end:
+        sql, args = sql + " AND observation_time<=?", args + [end]
+    rows = S.db.query(f"SELECT * FROM ({sql} ORDER BY observation_time DESC LIMIT ?) ORDER BY observation_time", tuple(args + [limit]))
+    return [_obs_row(r) for r in rows]
+
+
+# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ anomalies
+def _anom(r: dict) -> AnomalyOut:
+    return AnomalyOut(**{**r, "regional_evidence": bool(r["regional_evidence"]),
+                         "explanation": json.loads(r["explanation"]) if r["explanation"] else None})
+
+
+@app.get("/api/v1/anomalies", response_model=list[AnomalyOut])
+def anomalies(station_id: str | None = None, state: str | None = None, severity: str | None = None,

+        if val:
+            sql, args = sql + f" AND {col}=?", args + [val]
+    if not include_info:
+        sql += " AND state != 'INFO'"

+
+
+@app.get("/api/v1/anomalies/{anomaly_id}", response_model=AnomalyOut)
+def anomaly(anomaly_id: int):
+    rows = S.db.query("SELECT * FROM anomalies WHERE id=?", (anomaly_id,))
+    if not rows:
+        raise HTTPException(404, "anomaly not found")
+    return _anom(rows[0])
+
+
+@app.patch("/api/v1/anomalies/{anomaly_id}", response_model=AnomalyOut)
+def review_anomaly(anomaly_id: int, body: AnomalyUpdate):
+    """Operator review (acknowledge / mark false alarm). Only the review state changes."""
+    if not S.db.execute("UPDATE anomalies SET state=? WHERE id=? AND state!='INFO'", (body.state, anomaly_id)):
+        raise HTTPException(404, "anomaly not found")
+    return anomaly(anomaly_id)
+
+
+# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ metrics
+@app.get("/api/v1/metrics")
+def metrics():
+    now = time.time()
+    recent = [t for t in S.done_at if now - t <= 60]
+    proc = psutil.Process()
+    by = lambda col: {r["k"]: r["n"] for r in S.db.query(  # noqa: E731
+        f"SELECT {col} k, COUNT(*) n FROM anomalies WHERE state NOT IN ('INFO','RETRACTED') GROUP BY {col}")}
+    tot = S.db.query("SELECT COUNT(*) n, SUM(temperature_c IS NOT NULL AND pressure_hpa IS NOT NULL AND relative_humidity_pct IS NOT NULL) ok, "
+                     "SUM(delayed) delayed, SUM(out_of_order) ooo FROM observations")[0]
+    return {
+        "observations": tot["n"], "complete_observations_pct": 100 * (tot["ok"] or 0) / max(tot["n"], 1),
+        "delayed_observations": tot["delayed"] or 0, "out_of_order_observations": tot["ooo"] or 0,
+        "processing_latency_ms": latency_stats(list(S.latency)) if S.latency else None,
+        "end_to_end_latency_ms": latency_stats(list(S.e2e)) if S.e2e else None,
+        "throughput_obs_per_s_last_60s": len(recent) / 60.0,
+        "anomalies_by_station": by("station_id"), "anomalies_by_parameter": by("parameter"),
+        "anomalies_by_pattern": by("fault_pattern"), "anomalies_by_severity": by("severity"),
+        "review_states": {r["state"]: r["n"] for r in S.db.query("SELECT state, COUNT(*) n FROM anomalies GROUP BY state")},
+        "regional_events_suppressed": S.db.query("SELECT COUNT(*) n FROM anomalies WHERE state='INFO'")[0]["n"],
+        "cpu_percent": proc.cpu_percent(interval=None), "rss_mb": proc.memory_info().rss / 2**20,
+        "uptime_s": now - S.started, "detector_mode": S.engine.mode,
+        "health_trend": S.db.query("SELECT station_id, substr(observation_time,1,13) hour, AVG(health_score) health "

+    }
+
+

+@app.post("/api/v1/admin/reset")
+def admin_reset():

+    S.replay.stop()
+    S.reset()
+    return {"status": "reset"}
+
+
+@app.get("/api/v1/replay/scenarios")
+def scenarios():
+    return S.replay.scenarios()
+
+
+@app.get("/api/v1/replay/status")
+def replay_status():
+    return S.replay.status()
+
+
+@app.post("/api/v1/replay/start")
+def replay_start(body: ReplayStart):
+    if body.scenario not in S.replay.scenarios():
+        raise HTTPException(404, "unknown scenario")
+    return S.replay.start(body.scenario, body.speed, body.reset)
+
+
+@app.post("/api/v1/replay/stop")
+def replay_stop():
+    return S.replay.stop()
+
+
+@app.get("/api/v1/stream")
+async def stream(request: Request):
+    q: asyncio.Queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=2000)
+    S.subscribers.add(q)
+
+    async def gen():
+        try:
+            yield "event: hello\ndata: {}\n\n"
+            while not await request.is_disconnected():
+                try:
+                    yield await asyncio.wait_for(q.get(), timeout=15)
+                except asyncio.TimeoutError:
+                    yield ": keep-alive\n\n"
+        finally:
+            S.subscribers.discard(q)
+
+    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream", headers={"Cache-Control": "no-cache", "X-Accel-Buffering": "no"})
